title: {{NAME}} and the Field Between the Seasons
moral: The best teams are built not on who plays the best, but on who makes everyone around them believe they can.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a forest-green and silver soccer jersey with the number 10, deep green shorts with a silver stripe, and gleaming white soccer boots with silver laces.

pages.content: The Field Between the Seasons existed at the precise point where autumn became winter and winter had not yet decided to begin, which meant it was perpetually the most beautiful kind of afternoon: cool and gold and full of the smell of turned leaves and distant cold. The grass was a mixture of green and amber, and it was perfectly, impossibly flat. {{NAME}} arrived through a gap in a hawthorn hedge and found it already occupied. On one half of the field, a team of animals was practising: a leopard who played with absolute precision and a complete inability to share the ball, a capybara who was technically sound but deeply cautious, two young red foxes who were fast and enthusiastic and ran constantly into each other, and a dignified old tortoise in goal who had not moved yet but gave the impression that when he did, it would be entirely correct. On the pitch's edge, sitting on a toadstool with her wings folded and her expression one of concentrated distress, was the team's coach: a fairy named Flint, who had a clipboard the size of a postage stamp and a tactical problem she could see perfectly clearly and had no idea how to fix.

pages.content: Flint spotted {{NAME}} before he had taken three steps onto the pitch, which was impressive given that she was the size of a walnut. She flew directly to him, clipboard first, and delivered the situation report with the velocity of someone who has been waiting for someone to report it to. The team had a match the next morning against the Sky Meadow side, a team known for moving in coordinated formations so perfect they looked choreographed, which they were, because their coach was a starling who had written a book about it. Flint's team had talent in abundance. What they lacked was trust. The leopard trusted no one. The capybara trusted everyone so much she second-guessed herself constantly. The foxes trusted each other exclusively. The tortoise trusted the geometry of the goal and nothing else. {{NAME}} had played enough football to know that talent without trust was like a river without a channel: a lot of energy going nowhere in particular. He crouched on the grass and asked Flint something she had not thought to ask herself. What did each player love most about the game?

pages.content: Training was unlike anything the team had experienced before. {{NAME}} did not run drills. He asked questions. He asked the leopard to show him her fastest sprint, not toward goal, toward a teammate. He asked the capybara to call out what she saw from her position, every ten seconds, whatever it was. He asked the foxes to race each other to a single spot and then freeze: they arrived simultaneously, every time, and the moment they realised it they went very still with the expression of animals discovering something important about themselves. He ran plays where only the tortoise's positioning could unlock the goal, and the tortoise moved twice with an authority that silenced everyone. Flint buzzed in patterns above the pitch, her fairy-light casting a faint silver sheen on the moving players, and by the time the gold afternoon deepened toward evening, something had changed. The passes were finding people. The leopard had, once, deliberately laid the ball off. The capybara called a play that worked. The foxes split wide and both stayed there. It was not perfect. But it was becoming something.

pages.content: The match came at dawn, the sky the colour of a peach, and the Sky Meadow team arrived in matching sky-blue kits, moving in the fluid unison of a murmuration, their starling coach wheeling overhead calling adjustments in rapid, melodic bursts. For thirty minutes {{NAME}}'s team struggled to find their rhythm. The Sky Meadow passes were so precise they seemed to arrive before the players had moved. Then the capybara called out, loud and clear and without any hesitation at all: their formation has a gap, wide right, every third pass. Everyone heard it. The foxes split wide right. The leopard waited, just three seconds longer than was comfortable, and passed. The first fox took it, drew two defenders, and laid it to the second. Clean strike. Back of the net. The starling coach banked hard and called new instructions. The tortoise made two impossible saves. By the final whistle, {{NAME}}'s team had won by a single goal, and the capybara was sitting in the centre circle with both front paws over her face, overwhelmed in the best possible way. The leopard walked over and sat beside her, which was, for the leopard, the equivalent of a very long speech.

pages.content: After the match the Field Between the Seasons was quieter than before, the way a room is quieter after the best kind of party. The Sky Meadow team had stayed, and now animals from both sides were mixed together on the grass, the leopard and the fastest Sky Meadow player engaged in what appeared to be a technical conversation conducted entirely through demonstrations. The tortoise had finally moved away from his goal and was sitting in a patch of autumn sun with the satisfied air of a creature who has completed what it came to do. Flint perched on {{NAME}}'s knee, her wings finally still, her clipboard closed. She looked tired and enormously pleased. {{NAME}} lay back in the amber-green grass and stared at the peach-and-blue sky above, the chill of the field rising through his jersey like a gentle reminder to be present. His eyes went slow and heavy. The foxes were curled together nearby, already dozing. Sleep came for him softly, the way good things do. The field hummed and settled around him. Somewhere in the near distance, the capybara was talking to someone in a steady, confident voice. Tomorrow, {{NAME}} thought dreamily, she would have ideas about the next match. She had many ideas now.
